<reason>Both sides ran disciplined, well-shaped cases, but A repeatedly converted B's own material into support for CON. A turned the eurozone case (Greeks did vote in a referendum and still got austerity — "authorship was supplied; the constraint was material"), turned Venezuela (elected leaders dismantling counter-majoritarian safeguards that B relies on), and turned B's Ulysses image (self-binding is rational precisely because the rope is right and the will is wrong). A also landed a structural meta-argument that B never squarely neutralized: every virtue B claimed for legitimacy — compliance, durability, correction, feedback — is an outcome, which makes results the master criterion and competence the thing producing them. B's best live route, the means/ends distinction ("someone must decide whether price stability is worth unemployment"), was genuinely strong and well held into the closing, and B's "hired, scoped, revocable principal" reply to delegation was a real answer. But A's pressure question forced a damaging concession — B agreed a fully authorized policy that demonstrably raises child mortality is a bad decision — and A crystallized that cleanly: authorization is not what makes a public decision good. A also drew a usable distinction between "who may revoke" and "what weighs more in the deciding," blunting B's principal/agent frame. B's opening was clipped for exceeding the cap, a small execution cost, and B's closing largely restated the means/ends line without absorbing A's "ends-setting is itself competence-dependent" answer.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's handling of the delegation clash: B claimed independent central banks prove legitimacy hires competence, and A answered that a democracy's highest use of its own authority is to bind itself to expertise — then extended it via B's own Ulysses image, showing the mast only makes sense if being right outranks the sovereign's in-the-moment will. Paired with B's concession on the child-mortality hypothetical, this made A's "authorization cannot rescue a bad decision" the cleanest voting reason.</best_rebuttal>
